clinicalPearls: A genetically heterogeneous group of inherited anaemias united by ring sideroblasts in the marrow due to defective mitochondrial haem synthesis, iron-sulphur cluster biogenesis or wider mitochondrial metabolism
Divided into non-syndromic forms confined to erythropoiesis and syndromic forms with additional extra-haematological features
The commonest non-syndromic causes are ALAS2 (X-linked, often pyridoxine-responsive) and SLC25A38 (autosomal recessive, typically more severe and transfusion-dependent)

Syndromic forms include Pearson marrow-pancreas syndrome (mitochondrial DNA deletion with exocrine pancreatic failure), thiamine-responsive megaloblastic anaemia (SLC19A2, with diabetes and sensorineural deafness, Rogers syndrome), mitochondrial myopathy with lactic acidosis and sideroblastic anaemia (MLASA; PUS1, YARS2), sideroblastic anaemia with ataxia (ABCB7), and SIFD (TRNT1, with immunodeficiency, periodic fevers and developmental delay)
The anaemia is usually microcytic and hypochromic in haem-synthesis defects but may be normocytic or macrocytic in some mitochondrial or syndromic forms
Iron overload is common and treatment-limiting, occurring even without transfusion because of ineffective erythropoiesis, so iron therapy must be avoided
A pyridoxine trial is worthwhile, notably in ALAS2 disease, and thiamine benefits the SLC19A2 form; otherwise care centres on transfusion and iron chelation
Diagnosis integrates marrow morphology with Perls staining, the systemic phenotype and targeted gene or panel testing including mitochondrial DNA analysis
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital sideroblastic anaemias arise from inherited defects that impair the terminal mitochondrial steps of haem synthesis (for example ALAS2, and SLC25A38 which supplies mitochondrial glycine), iron-sulphur cluster assembly and export (GLRX5, ABCB7), or broader mitochondrial function including mitochondrial DNA integrity, RNA processing and translation (Pearson syndrome, PUS1, YARS2, TRNT1) and thiamine-dependent metabolism (SLC19A2). The common end point is failure to incorporate iron delivered to the erythroblast mitochondrion into protoporphyrin and haem, so iron accumulates in perinuclear mitochondria to form ring sideroblasts. Impaired haemoglobinisation and ineffective erythropoiesis produce anaemia, while hepcidin suppression drives systemic iron overload, and syndromic forms add multisystem features reflecting the affected mitochondrial or metabolic pathway.
additionalDifferentials: Acquired clonal sideroblastic anaemia (myelodysplasia with ring sideroblasts)
Iron-deficiency anaemia and thalassaemia, the other microcytic anaemias
Reversible acquired sideroblastic change from alcohol, isoniazid and other drugs, lead, or copper deficiency including zinc excess
Congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia and other inherited disorders of ineffective erythropoiesis
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film, often showing a dimorphic hypochromic microcytic picture
Bone marrow aspirate with Perls stain for ring sideroblasts, and trephine to assess dysplasia
Iron studies with raised ferritin and transferrin saturation, to exclude iron deficiency
Congenital sideroblastic anaemia gene panel (ALAS2, SLC25A38, GLRX5, ABCB7, PUS1, YARS2, SLC19A2, TRNT1) and mitochondrial DNA analysis for Pearson syndrome
Blood lead, copper and zinc, with assessment for alcohol and drug causes
Investigation of syndromic features including lactate, pancreatic exocrine function, audiometry, glucose tolerance and neurological assessment
Hepatic and cardiac iron quantification by MRI (T2*)
redFlags: Iron overload with cardiac, hepatic or endocrine failure
Pancytopenia, lactic acidosis or multiorgan involvement suggesting Pearson or another mitochondrial syndrome
Transfusion-dependence with faltering growth in infancy
Recurrent fevers with immunodeficiency, suggesting TRNT1-related SIFD
reference.prognosis: Outlook varies widely by genotype: vitamin-responsive forms (ALAS2, SLC19A2) may do well, whereas SLC25A38 and many syndromic or mitochondrial forms are severe, and Pearson syndrome in particular carries a poor prognosis. Iron overload is a major and largely preventable cause of morbidity across the group.
pitfalls: Treating the anaemia as iron deficiency and giving iron, which worsens overload
Failing to look for a syndromic or mitochondrial diagnosis, for example missing Pearson syndrome
Not trialling pyridoxine or thiamine where the genotype makes it relevant
Assuming ring sideroblasts always indicate myelodysplasia in a young patient
Underestimating non-transfusional iron loading and its complications
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
management: Trial pyridoxine in ALAS2-related X-linked disease, which is frequently vitamin-responsive, and thiamine in SLC19A2 (thiamine-responsive megaloblastic anaemia)
Avoid iron supplementation entirely, since ineffective erythropoiesis already drives systemic iron overload
Support transfusion-dependent forms (typically SLC25A38 and severe syndromic disease) with red-cell transfusion while treating the resulting and pre-existing iron loading with chelation therapy
Monitor iron burden with serial ferritin and transferrin saturation and with cardiac and hepatic iron imaging to guide chelation
Consider allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation in severe, transfusion-dependent, non-responsive disease as the only curative option
Identify and manage syndromic features — diabetes and sensorineural deafness in Rogers syndrome, exocrine pancreatic failure in Pearson syndrome, and the immunodeficiency and periodic fevers of SIFD
Offer genetic counselling and family testing given the inherited basis
